source_metadata.title: An End-to-End Agent Auditing Engine
source_metadata.source_type: arXiv preprint; software/agent-evaluation framework with empirical harness benchmark study

atoms.canonical_statement: A2E is introduced as an end-to-end evaluation engine for systematically auditing agent harnesses.
A2E uses the Agent Task Protocol (ATP) to decouple benchmark adaptation from agent-harness execution so benchmarks and harnesses can be composed without pairwise integration code.
A2E's Monitor builds on OpenInference and records agent execution with OpenTelemetry-compatible spans.
A2E's Evaluation Layer registers each metric under an execution stage and a fine-grained evaluation dimension in a Lifecycle-Aligned Evaluation taxonomy.
A2E stores trajectories, metric definitions, and evaluation results in a database to support persistent, incremental, and longitudinal evaluation across runs.
The authors report that no harness-model configuration is universally dominant across the evaluated tasks.
The authors report that endpoint correctness alone has limited resolution for distinguishing harnesses because process and operational metrics can differ more strongly.
Harness effectiveness is characterized as model- and task-dependent rather than globally rankable.
The Task Layer organizes benchmarks in a hierarchical tree indexed by time, category, and difficulty.
Each benchmark execution-support bundle contains a sandbox definition, task dataset, experiment configuration, and runtime environment.
The unified access component normalizes heterogeneous representative-agent and SDK-based agent interfaces into a common agent-access abstraction and attaches the same monitor to each agent.
During the monitor loop, A2E captures model calls, state transitions, errors, tool calls, latency, token consumption, and generated artifacts.
Agent runs are represented as ordered reasoning-action-observation event sequences that preserve both final outcomes and intermediate decisions.

The Evaluation Layer combines outcome evaluation with trajectory evaluation so inefficient, unsafe, or otherwise undesirable execution behavior can be assessed in addition to final-answer correctness.
Rule-based evaluators compute accuracy, task success rate, tool success rate, latency, token usage, cost, and trajectory-step counts.
LLM-as-judge evaluators score final-result quality, reasoning quality, tool-use quality, instruction following, relevance and completeness, and safety.
The centralized database organizes structured evaluation records into trajectory, result, and metric stores that are queryable across benchmarks, agents, models, and configurations.
A2E's runtime pipeline is divided into Task, Server, Evaluation, and UI components, with the server acting as the coordination point for experiment data.
The A2E user interface is intentionally read-only: it displays traces and scores but does not launch experiments or modify evaluation records.
Monitor instrumentation is separated into semantic, span, and SDK layers that respectively define behavior semantics, record bounded operations, and adapt framework-specific runtime events.
The span layer records start and end times, context, status, and parent-child relationships so an agent run is represented as related operations rather than a flat log sequence.
A2E adopts the OpenTelemetry span model in which related spans share a trace identity and parent-child relationships encode causal execution structure.
Span-based tracing is designed to expose delays, failure locations, reasoning paths, model consultations, and external capability use that cannot be recovered from the final response alone.
ATP is an internal software protocol that defines the task representation, agent-facing interface, and execution record used by the Task Layer.

ATP is implemented with TaskInput, AgentBinding, AgentRunner, and TaskTrace objects; TaskInput carries task data, AgentBinding supplies tools and prompts, AgentRunner executes the task, and TaskTrace records the normalized result.
The registered harnesses are Agno, AutoGen AgentChat, CrewAI, Google ADK, LangGraph, LlamaIndex, OpenAI Agents SDK, Smolagents, and the Anthropic Python SDK.
Registry support does not imply that every framework-benchmark pair has passed end-to-end validation.
The report groups 23 benchmarks into coding, conversational, research, and computer-use task areas.
Dataset adapters support text, tool-use, and sandbox tasks while preserving the same ATP boundary to the agent harness.
Trajectory generation begins from a benchmark key, harness key, and model name; the registry resolves the dataset loader, binding, runner, and SDK mapping.
The CLI samples 40 candidate tasks without replacement by default; users may choose another sample size or provide a random seed, and the CLI creates a seed when none is supplied.
TaskTrace stores run status, turn count, ordered tool calls, final answer, elapsed time, and raw framework output, and can be linked by trace identifier to the runtime span tree.
A2E provides a native ExperimentRunner path and a CLI run_experiment path for trajectory generation; both follow ATP but differ in orchestration and root-span ownership.
Each CLI run records agent framework, model, SDK, dataset key, sample seed, and selected task identifiers; reproduction also requires the same dataset version, model endpoint, and run settings.
The Lifecycle-Aligned Evaluation taxonomy contains four stages: Reasoning, Action, Final Answer, and Runtime Quality.

Reasoning is divided into Task, Flow, and Logical dimensions; Action into Tool, Skill, and Memory; Final Answer into Answer Correctness and Task Completion; Runtime Quality into Efficiency and Safety.
The framework separates process-level evaluation of reasoning/actions, outcome-level evaluation of the final result, and lifecycle-level evaluation of operational properties.
The metric catalog is explicitly not intended as a complete definition of agent quality.
Each metric is registered to a lifecycle stage and dimension while its implementation may use an LLM judge, deterministic rule, environment verifier, or statistical aggregation function.
New metrics can be added under an existing lifecycle dimension without modifying the benchmark runner, agent harness, or existing metrics.
Evaluation operates over task-level database records containing task, agent configuration, turns, model outputs, tool calls, execution status, errors, resource usage, and other trajectory evidence.
Separating trajectory generation from metric computation allows stored trajectories to be re-evaluated with new metrics, judge models, or aggregation policies without rerunning the agent.
Large auxiliary artifacts may remain in external file or object storage while their identifiers and locations are indexed in the database.

atoms.canonical_statement: Figure 1 shows substantially wider cross-harness variation in planning, tool use, safety, and efficiency metrics than in final-answer correctness.
In the main harness-benchmark matrix, all nine harnesses use the same DeepSeek-V4-pro (FP4) backbone model, inference settings, tool setup, step limit, and timeout budget.
Each benchmark contributes five tasks from a fixed seed, and every harness receives the identical task IDs so harness runs are aligned by task rather than independently sampled.
The full evaluation matrix contains 1,035 scored runs across 23 benchmarks.

atoms.canonical_statement: On the single-turn tasks highlighted by the authors—ARC-Challenge, GSM8K, OpenBookQA, and HumanEval—harness choice produced identical or nearly identical final-outcome scores across the nine harnesses.
The authors emphasize larger harness separation on multi-turn tasks, including τ-bench, GDPVal, and Traject-Bench.
OpenAI Agents scores 1.00 on Traject-Bench but 0.20 on τ-bench and 0.00 on GDPVal, illustrating that harness rankings do not transfer consistently across tasks.
Across the 19 non-sandbox benchmarks alone, LlamaIndex averages 0.77 correctness versus 0.74 for Agno, whereas on the full 23-benchmark average Agno leads 0.68 to 0.64.

atoms.canonical_statement: Because each Table 1 cell is based on only five tasks, score resolution is 0.20 and the authors state that per-cell variance is high.
The authors state that Table 1 is not intended to rank the frameworks; its purpose is to demonstrate that the full harness-benchmark grid executes and scores end-to-end in one pipeline.

atoms.canonical_statement: Figure 6 re-scores correctness on 44 runs for which the multiple-choice extractor returned an empty prediction.
CrewAI is omitted from Figure 6's token-cost plot because its LLM spans do not carry token counts.
The Figure 6 rows for tool_invocation and hallucination are set by instrumentation rather than by the agent and should not be interpreted as harness behavior.
The authors report that the remaining process dimensions move little on the evaluated benchmark mix and leave conversion of those metrics into concrete harness-design guidance to future work.
The cross-benchmark comparison evaluates nine harnesses on GDPVal, MMLU-Pro, and τ3-bench with GLM-5.2 fixed as the common API model.
For Figure 7, harness quality is scored by normalized distance to a high-success, low-token 'sweet spot' using Q_h = 1 - sqrt(T_hat_h^2 + (1 - S_hat_h)^2) / sqrt(2).
The top three harnesses by the Figure 7 success-efficiency score are CrewAI, OpenAI Agents, and AutoGen AgentChat on GDPVal.
The top three harnesses by the Figure 7 success-efficiency score are OpenAI Agents, AutoGen AgentChat, and LangGraph on MMLU-Pro.
The top three harnesses by the Figure 7 success-efficiency score are LangGraph, Claude-Agent-SDK, and Google ADK on τ3-bench.
The reported harness success-rate gap on GDPVal is 0.20.

atoms.canonical_statement: Figure 7 shows that no single harness consistently dominates all three benchmarks under the same GLM-5.2 model backend.

The authors conclude that harness design choices—including prompt construction, tool representation, context management, execution loops, error handling, and termination policies—can materially change agent behavior even when the underlying model is fixed.
The case study compares LangGraph and CrewAI on exactly the same τ3-bench task using the same GLM-5.2 model and initial environment.

source_consistency_issues.description: Table 2 on page 14 labels the LangGraph trajectory as successful but lists correctness=0.0, while the Section 6.3 narrative on the same page states that LangGraph obtains correctness=1.0. Both source reports are retained as separate atoms.

extraction_limitations: Pages 16-18 are bibliography pages and were inspected for source context but not atomized as evidence.
No standalone funding disclosure, conflict-of-interest statement, or data-availability statement was identified in the provided 18-page preprint, so no atoms of those kinds were created.

The paper has no dedicated limitations section; limitation atoms are restricted to explicit source statements about validation boundaries, metric scope, sample resolution/variance, missing token instrumentation, instrumentation-defined metrics, and future-work limits.
Table 2 and the Section 6.3 narrative conflict on the LangGraph case-study correctness value (0.0 versus 1.0); the extraction preserves both rather than reconciling them.
The extraction records source-reported benchmark and trajectory results but does not independently verify the linked repository, benchmark implementations, model endpoints, or runtime traces.
schema_note: Each object in atoms validates independently against literature_atom.schema.json; the outer wrapper is an extraction report and is not itself a LiteratureAtom.
